analysis.one_liner: Treats US-controlled corporations chartered in tax-haven countries as domestic companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 25, 2007, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: When a US-owned company sets up a subsidiary in a tax-haven country like the Cayman Islands or Bermuda, current rules let it defer paying US tax on profits parked there. This bill would simply treat those subsidiaries as domestic corporations, so profits shifted offshore would be taxed the same as profits earned at home. It contained an exception for subsidiaries doing real business in the haven country itself, not just bookkeeping operations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who ultimately make up tax revenue lost when multinationals shift profits into low-tax countries, and domestic companies that compete against haven-using rivals without the benefit of offshore subsidiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Controlled foreign corporations organized in tax-haven countries would be taxed as domestic corporations, so their profits could no longer sit offshore untaxed indefinitely.
The bill listed dozens of specific haven jurisdictions, from the Cayman Islands to Bermuda, and let the Treasury Secretary add or remove countries as the problem evolved.

It exempted subsidiaries earning substantially all their income from real business activity inside the haven country, limiting the measure to shell-style arrangements rather than genuine foreign operations.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational companies that use subsidiaries in tax havens to defer or avoid US tax on foreign-shifted income, and the small army of accountants, lawyers, and financial firms that build those structures.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue that treating haven subsidiaries as domestic corporations could double-tax genuinely foreign income and put US multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors who face no comparable rules.
Companies facing the tax could respond by moving real operations, headquarters, or ownership abroad rather than paying US tax, which could cost American jobs rather than raise revenue.
The effective date was set for taxable years after December 31, 2008, meaning the bill would not have produced revenue until well after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taxing profits parked in tax havens the same as profits earned at home — addresses a real and persistent drain on the treasury, and the carve-out for genuinely local business shows the drafters tried to avoid punishing real foreign investment. But the blunt approach carries real risks of companies relocating actual operations abroad, and other narrower anti-haven proposals could capture much of the revenue with less disruption. On balance, the public interest in closing the loophole outweighed the adjustment costs, though the design would have needed refinement in committee — a process that never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on January 25, 2007, joined by Senators Levin and Feingold, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.

The Senate Finance Committee held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 110th Congress; the only actions after referral were two sets of sponsor introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record.
The bill attracted five cosponsors (four Democrats and one Independent) and died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2009 without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinationals that rely on tax-haven subsidiaries kept the ability to defer US tax on profits shifted offshore, since no committee ever took up the bill.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to six senators.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

against.name: US multinational corporations using offshore tax-haven structures
against.role: Beneficiaries of the existing deferral rules
against.what_they_did: The bill's targets had a strong interest in the status quo; tax-haven use by US companies was a well-documented and contested issue during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters were Democrats or the Independent Sanders, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined; with a Democratic-led Finance Committee declining to act, the bill faced no recorded floor opposition because it never got that far.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to defer US tax on profits routed through haven countries, directly costing the companies that use these structures. Their savings come at the expense of the general taxpayer, so their interest runs against ordinary people in this bill.

industries.industry: Tax-haven financial and incorporation services (Cayman Islands, Bermuda, etc.)
industries.note: These jurisdictions and the legal and accounting firms that serve them build the shell structures the bill targets; treating haven subsidiaries as domestic corporations would shrink demand for their services.

industries.industry: Domestic US businesses without offshore structures
industries.note: Companies that pay full US tax and compete against haven-using rivals would face a more level playing field if the loophole closed.
